questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I decided course selection would be my priority number one, besides the fact I knew I would pick either Canada or USA (and to a lesser extent Australia or New Zealand) due to my specific topics of interest in Indigenous peoples in settler colonial nations.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Most often I would just look in my mail, but finding information wasn't the trickiest part, more so it was feeling I knew all the things I had to or had done all I had to.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Firstly, there was an orientation about two weeks in where they told you everything, but almost all of it had been told to you before arriving. Was an opportunity to meet more exchange students, though. 
You get frequent mail from University of Toronto about opportunities for meeting other exchange students at certain events and the first couple weeks there are some booths around campus where they give flyers for the same type of thing. I did not go to any, however, as it was unnecessary for me.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It really wasn't very easy and most people I spoke to had some complaints about the places they ended up staying.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Make sure to apply early to off-campus housing options like Tartu College or others like it. If you do it when you get your acceptance letter, you're a bit late in the process - like I was and did not get a mail back from them until I was finishing my stay.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You just fill out a google form for each course you want to apply to and you can apply to 5 if you want and drop one later. In the google form you just write the course you want and what courses you have taken previously that should grant you access (fulfil prerequisite requirements).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always write them an email. I did so when I didn't know how to read the course codes and found out Y courses were for the full year (2 semesters) so I could not take them as I was there for one semester.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to also ask for permission from UCPH for more than just what you need so you have options if there are many you are interested in.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It can feel very unclear what is required to pass a class, but in the end it wasn't too bad and I was nowhere near not passing in any of my courses. Even after subpar performances in some assignments or midterm tests. This does not mean they won't be complicated as I had one course where the professor kept using the most unusual words instead of more normal synonyms. I spoke to the Canadian students and even they had to google most of the words from the readings and lectures.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There are grand auditorium lectures as well as smaller 20-person classes so it's a mix of things most have tried before. In some courses they offer a lot more freedom than others like one course where the assignments were in a topic of your own choosing, disconnected from the lecture topics. Another class didn't have any exams because the teacher didn't believe exams were beneficial.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ANT318H1 - The Preindustrial City and Urban Social Theory
LIN202H1 - Introduction to Indigenous Languages of the Americas
JPI201H1 - Indigenous Politics in Canada
FAH255H1: Art of Indigenous North America

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would wholeheartedly recommend JPI201 - Indigenous Politics in Canada as it very much shaped my experience and my relation to Canada and to a lesser extent Denmark as well. When speaking to Canadians it is very obvious the Indigenous peoples are not given much thought from day to day and their suffering is ignored and ignorance is uncontested. I believe anyone studying in Canada should take this course or one like it to understand the country they are studying in. It is also quite entry-level I would say as you do not need to know the name of a singly Indigenous group or anything about Political Science theory. + no exams!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My costs ^ are not necessarily super accurate, but I paid more than necessary for food because I ordered out a lot because of 1) my kitchen was in poor condition and 2) food opportunities in Toronto are very tasty.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Prices aren't so different from Denmark. If you go watch varsity matches it is entirely free for students so it was a frequent way to meetup with other exchange students.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of different clubs you can be a part of and most don't even require you to sign up, you just show up. I spoke to some who went on camping trips and I went to board game club every Wednesday evening.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you have any hobbies at home in Denmark I recommend you check if they have a club for it as it's likely they do and if you don't have a lot of roommates or travelled with someone the social activities really feel so refreshing. I felt so much lighter and better after board game club (GLG). A lot of people there weren't board game nerds or playing big complex board games, it was mostly party game type games and social games. I made a lot of friends there and the friends I made outside of it I would bring so we could hang out there.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to Houston and Dallas in the reading week which should just be treated as a vacation week. This does not mean I recommend Texas, just to say it makes sense to visit other spots in North America now that you're so close. If you haven't been you should visit Niagara Falls and most Canadians recommended people visit Banff and Halifax.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Took a couple weeks to get used to the baffling amount of homeless people, but just don't interact and they are harmless.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In class they often sit with people they already know, so it is most easy to seek out the other exchange students. In clubs, however, it is easy to socialize with locals as they are most of the attendants. There they are also more welcoming.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It wasn't very challenging. If anything, when they get angry they often end sentences in "eh?" which can be hard not to laugh at in serious situations.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I found a lot of people really liked that you were from somewhere else even if their parents were 1st generation immigrants. It was fun to feel special for something completely out of your control.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Go to a club, interact with Indigenous opportunities like Native Canadian Centre of Toronto just off campus, and relax - enjoy your stay you will pass just focus on learning and getting something out of it, and not being perfect in your classes.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Robarts Library is a great study space. In the evenings you can find raccoons around campus and in Queen's Park just off campus.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I loved my courses.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Just getting used to my housing.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
